what_its_for: Erythromycin ethylsuccinate is an antibiotic used to treat a variety of bacterial infections, including ear infections, throat infections (such as strep throat), skin infections, pneumonia, and certain sexually transmitted infections. It works by stopping bacteria from growing and multiplying. It will NOT work for viral infections like the common cold or flu.
how_to_take: Take this medicine exactly as your doctor or pharmacist tells you. It comes as a liquid (suspension) or tablet. You can take it with or without food, but taking it with food may help reduce stomach upset. If you are taking the liquid form, shake the bottle well before each use and measure your dose carefully using the measuring cup or spoon that comes with the medicine — do not use a regular kitchen spoon. Swallow tablets whole; do not crush or chew them unless your doctor says it is okay. Finish the entire course of treatment even if you start to feel better, to make sure the infection is completely cleared.
dosing: The dose your doctor prescribes will depend on your age, weight, and the type of infection being treated. A common adult dose is 400 mg taken every 6 hours (4 times a day), or 800 mg taken every 12 hours (twice a day), for 7 to 14 days. Children's doses are usually based on body weight and are given 2 to 4 times a day. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and never adjust your dose without talking to your healthcare provider first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular dosing schedule. Do NOT double up or take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store tablets and unopened liquid bottles at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C), away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Keep them out of the bathroom medicine cabinet. Once the liquid suspension is mixed or opened, store it in the refrigerator and use it within 10 days — do not freeze it. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medicine after the expiration date printed on the label. Dispose of any unused medicine safely by following your local pharmacy take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking antacids that contain aluminum or magnesium at the same time as erythromycin, as they can reduce how well the medicine works — space them apart by at least 2 hours. Do not take with certain other medicines without checking with your doctor or pharmacist first, including blood thinners (like warfarin), statins (cholesterol medicines), certain heart rhythm medicines, or ergotamine (used for migraines), as serious interactions can occur. Avoid drinking large amounts of grapefruit juice while on this medication. Do not share this antibiotic with anyone else, even if they have similar symptoms.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency medical help if you experience: a severe allergic reaction (rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing); severe stomach pain, cramping, or bloody diarrhea (which could be a sign of a serious gut infection called C. difficile); fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat or chest pain; yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe nausea (signs of liver problems); or hearing loss or ringing in the ears. Also contact your doctor if your symptoms do not improve after a few days or if they get worse.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within 2 to 3 days of starting this antibiotic. However, it is very important to finish the entire prescribed course of treatment — usually 7 to 14 days — even if you feel completely well. Stopping early can allow the bacteria to come back and may make the infection harder to treat in the future.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Erythromycin is generally considered safe during pregnancy and is sometimes prescribed when other antibiotics cannot be used. It does pass into breast milk in small amounts, but it is usually considered safe for breastfeeding mothers — always tell your doctor if you are pregnant or nursing. Children: This medicine is commonly used in children, with doses based on body weight. The liquid suspension form is often preferred for young children. Older adults: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects, especially hearing-related problems or heart rhythm changes — your doctor may monitor you more closely. Liver disease: If you have liver problems, tell your doctor before taking this medicine, as erythromycin is processed by the liver and may need to be used with caution or at a lower dose.
